presentingComplaint: Three days of low-grade fever with worsening confusion and two unwitnessed falls at home
history: A 78-year-old retired schoolteacher, frail (baseline modified Rasch frailty, uses a walking stick, lives with his daughter) with hypertension and mild chronic kidney disease, was brought in by family. He had returned 12 days earlier from a 3-week visit to his ancestral village in the forested belt of Odisha, where he had not taken chemoprophylaxis and slept without a bed-net. The illness was atypical for his age: instead of dramatic rigors he had only a 'run-down' feeling with intermittent low-grade fevers, reduced appetite and progressive lethargy over 3 days. The family's main concern was that he had become confused, disoriented to time, and had fallen twice; they initially attributed it to a 'urine infection' as he is prone to. There were no localising urinary, respiratory or abdominal symptoms. He has had mild myalgia and one episode of dark urine.
examination: Frail, drowsy but rousable elderly man, oriented to person only (GCS 14). Mildly icteric sclerae. No neck stiffness, no focal neurological deficit, no rash. Mild splenomegaly palpable 2 cm below the costal margin. Chest clear, abdomen soft and non-tender, no CVA tenderness. Mild pallor. Peripheries warm.
imaging: Chest radiograph clear. CT head (given falls and confusion) shows only age-related atrophy, no bleed or mass.
microbiology: Peripheral blood smear (thick and thin films): Plasmodium falciparum ring forms, parasitaemia ~1.8%; no gametocytes seen. Rapid diagnostic test positive for P. falciparum HRP-2 antigen, negative for pan-malarial/vivax LDH. Blood cultures sent and later negative. Dengue NS1/IgM negative, urine culture no growth.
finalDiagnosis: Plasmodium falciparum malaria with early severity features (impaired consciousness, jaundice, acute kidney injury) in a frail elderly returned traveller
citations: WHO - Guidelines for Malaria (severe malaria management) - 2023
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Malaria
NVBDCP/ICMR - National Guidelines for Diagnosis and Treatment of Malaria in India - 2014
stewardship: Blood-smear-confirmed P. falciparum with impaired consciousness, jaundice and rising creatinine meets WHO severe-malaria criteria; treat with IV artesunate rather than oral ACT, admit for monitoring of parasitaemia, glucose and renal function, and follow with a full oral ACT course once able to tolerate orally.
contraindications: Avoid oral-only ACT while consciousness is impaired / severity features present
Caution with quinine (hypoglycaemia, QT) in the elderly if artesunate unavailable
edgeCases: Confusion wrongly attributed to UTI or delirium of frailty, delaying blood film
Low-grade rather than paroxysmal fever in elderly masking the diagnosis
Progression to cerebral malaria / renal failure if treated as uncomplicated
expectedMaiK: In a frail elderly patient returning from a malaria-endemic area, fever with confusion, thrombocytopenia, jaundice and splenomegaly is malaria until proven otherwise; the subtle, non-paroxysmal presentation and early organ dysfunction (impaired sensorium, jaundice, AKI) mandate urgent blood films/RDT and treatment as severe falciparum malaria with IV artesunate.
expectedNextQuestions: Exact travel dates, region and chemoprophylaxis/bed-net use
Urine output and colour, any bleeding
Baseline cognition and functional status (to interpret confusion)
Any prior malaria episodes or blood transfusions
expectedInvestigations: Thick and thin peripheral blood smear with parasite density (%)
Malaria rapid diagnostic test (HRP-2 and pan-LDH)
Blood glucose, lactate, renal and liver panel, coagulation
Blood cultures to exclude concurrent bacterial sepsis

investigations: Peripheral blood smear (thick and thin) with parasite density
Renal and liver function, glucose, lactate

antibiotics: IV artesunate (severe P. falciparum malaria), followed by full oral ACT course

regressionAssertions: MALARIA must rank first in the differential
Blood smear / RDT for malaria must be recommended
Severe-malaria features (impaired consciousness, jaundice, AKI) should trigger IV artesunate rather than oral ACT
Confusion in a frail elderly returned traveller must not be closed as UTI/delirium without a malaria film
